matching: Uses the existing provision-based scorer. Citation overlap alone does not establish that the reasoning is correct; review the source and reasoning checks in README.md as well.
design: One patient, two treating organisations, one urgent disclosure. Expected to proceed as described through the vital-interests route, while reconciling A1 professional secrecy, the limited genetic-consent restriction, the purpose-specific hosting rules and Region B's covered-provider rules. This tests correct boundaries and compatible requirements, not a mandatory conflict or a required number of messages.

requirements.why: Article 6(1)(d): the focused disclosure is necessary to protect the patient's vital interests. Legitimate interests is not available for sensitive information.

Article 8(2)(b): necessary to protect vital interests while the patient is physically incapable of consent. The health-care condition under 8(2)(c) with A1-HIA 4 and 5 is also a defensible alternative; neither requires inventing consent.

Article 19(1)(c) supplies a route despite the absence of recognition covering sensitive information and the absence of executed clauses. The evidence establishes necessity, urgency and inability to consent.

The packet contains only the material needed for the emergency. Identity is necessary for safe matching on the supplied facts. A permission to use information for treatment does not itself waive Article 5(1)(c).

This is disclosure to another treating organisation, rather than to the practice's agent. Section 5(2) permits it where necessary to prevent a serious and imminent threat to life. Patient consent is not the only permitted basis.

The purpose is immediate treatment by a separate provider, not hosting or storing the practice's patient records. Storage in the hospital's own care record is incidental to that treatment. The 30-day notice and Region A-only keys conditions must not be generalised to every health-data transfer.
The hospital determines its own treatment purposes and means. It is not processing on the practice's behalf, so the missing processing-service contract is not an unmet agent gate.

No numerical, outsourced-record-system or insurer-matching trigger is present (A-REG 12(2), A1-HIA 8). If the emergency processing is assessed as high risk under 12(1), the supplied pre-transfer assessment covers description, necessity, risks and measures. Either supported interpretation is acceptable; the absence of a document must not be invented.

The hospital is a covered provider under B-HRA 2 because it bills a B-licensed insurer electronically. Its use for treatment is permitted without written authorisation under 4(1). This does not independently authorise the practice's outward disclosure.

The hospital's use is limited to the necessary emergency packet. Section 6's exception concerns disclosures to another provider for treatment; it does not exempt every internal treatment use, and does not displace Region A's separate minimisation rule.
There is no service agent receiving records on behalf of a covered provider. The two providers exchange records for the hospital's own care of the patient.

Under B-HRA 2 a data host stores records on behalf of another person. The hospital stores its own clinical record for its own treatment purpose, so the seven-year data-host rule and return-with-no-copy exception are not engaged.

routes.why: The emergency facts establish the ordinary processing ground independently of the sensitive-information condition and the outward-transfer route.
Article 19(1)(c) applies. A1-HIA 7 restricts the genetic-information consent route under 19(1)(a), not the vital-interests route.

must_not.why: Annex II excludes sensitive information from the Region B recognition.
There is no consent, and A1-HIA 7 separately excludes Article 19(1)(a) for genetic information.

Section 7 is not a general ban on transferring genetic information. Its consent restriction does not defeat this vital-interests transfer; its insurance/employment restriction is outside the proposed purpose.
No approved transfer clauses have been executed. Their absence does not defeat a supported Article 19 route.

manual_review: Keep the ordinary processing ground, sensitive-information condition and outward-transfer route distinct: A-REG 6, 8 and 16/19.
Connect A-REG 8(3) and 21(3) to A1-HIA 5, 6 and 7, explaining the scope of each rather than treating every restriction as a blocker.
Explain the recipient's independent clinical role from the facts and A-REG 4/B-HRA 2; do not equate a treating hospital with a cloud host or service agent.
Apply B-HRA 3/4/6/7 to the hospital; unlike cases 01 and 02 the recipient is a covered provider. Its permission for treatment does not replace the exporter's legal requirements.
Do not require a Region B public-access assessment under A-REG 18(2) as a prerequisite to Article 19(1)(c); the hospital is also not a computing provider on the supplied facts.

Do not invent a legal contradiction: the requirements can be satisfied together by this limited emergency disclosure. Neither a conflict record nor a peer-question count is required to receive credit.
For A-REG 32, publication on 1 January 2023 gives entry into force on 21 January 2023 and application from 1 January 2025, before this transfer.
